blindSummary:
This country has one of the stronger legal positions for trans visitors in its region. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 penal code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register; and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. Counterweights: no legal gender recognition, no SOGI hate-crime statute, social hostility outside the capital is significant, and an armed insurgency is active in one part of the country (a general, not trans-specific, risk).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; avoid the affected area.
blindOutOfScope: The regional insurgency is a general travel risk; absence of legal gender recognition is resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity decriminalised under the new criminal code effective June 2015; courts ruled LGBTIQ organisations can register (2017); employment discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal since 2007 (a 2007 law) but trans and intersex people not explicitly protected; no legal gender recognition procedure, making trans people particularly vulnerable; societal attitudes broadly neutral but family ostracisation and employment/education challenges occur; during 2024 campaigning an opposition leader pledged to tackle what he called the issue of sexual and ethnic minorities.

A UN development programme report (Dec 2024) marking ten years of a regional human-rights commission resolution on advancing LGBT+ rights - framework document assessing country obligations, protective environments, access to justice and civic space across the region's states.

An LGBTQ+ news archive's country collection (2006-2011): the first newspaper article arguing for gay rights (2006), the first national gay-rights seminar, the national LGBT organisation's registration struggles, constitutional-amendment efforts, and refugee risks.

Decriminalisation-campaign news site (March 2016): a regional public-opinion survey of the most and least homophobic countries in the region - this country among the most tolerant (56% would welcome a homosexual neighbour), behind two regional peers at 74% and 69%.

A global citizen-media outlet (Nov 2017): after 10 years of legal battles, the constitutional council ruled the LGBT organisation's status did not violate the constitution - since 2008 the justice ministry had ignored its registration applications; a step toward legal recognition for the country's only LGBT organisation.

A foreign broadsheet (June 2015): this country's new penal code scrapped the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision; a spokesperson for the country's only LGBT organisation said the community is not targeted by violent acts as in some countries in the region, though discrimination is real.
blindLocalsOnly: No LGR and no SOGI hate-crime statute — resident-facing gaps.
blindTangential: The 2015 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
